topics.title: Functions: parameters, return and scope
topics.intro: A function is a named, reusable block of code. You pass values in through parameters and get a result back with return. Variables made inside a function are local: they vanish when it ends, which stops one part of a program accidentally breaking another.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between a parameter and an argument.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which jobs in a game {she} would turn into functions.

topics.title: Dictionaries
topics.intro: A dictionary stores pairs: a key and its value, like a word and its meaning, or a god and their symbol. Instead of remembering a position, you look things up by name.
topics.teach: Explain when a dictionary is better than a list.
topics.talk: Ask {him} how {she} would store everyone’s phone numbers in Python.

topics.title: Strings: methods, slicing and f-strings
topics.intro: Strings come with built-in methods: count, find, replace, split, join. Slicing picks out parts, and f-strings drop values neatly into text. Most real programs spend a lot of time handling text.
topics.teach: Explain what split() and join() do.
topics.talk: Ask {her} to reverse a word in Python in one line.

topics.title: Nested loops and 2D lists
topics.intro: A list of lists makes a grid: a game board, a seating plan, Daedalus’s labyrinth or the pixels of an image. A loop inside a loop visits every square, row by row.
topics.teach: Explain how grid[2][3] finds one square.
topics.talk: Draw a 3 × 3 noughts-and-crosses board as a Python list of lists together.

topics.title: Validation and robust programs
topics.intro: Users type the strangest things. Robust programs check input (validation), confirm it was entered correctly (verification), and are tested with normal, boundary and erroneous data so they never crash.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between validation and verification.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what checks a sign-up form should make.

topics.title: Files: saving and loading data
topics.intro: Variables disappear when a program ends. To keep high scores or settings, programs write data to files and read it back next time. Opening a file the wrong way can wipe it, so the mode matters.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between opening a file with "w" and with "a".
topics.talk: Ask {her} which apps on {her} phone must save data to files.

topics.title: Random numbers and simulations
topics.intro: Games, simulations and encryption all need randomness. Python’s random module can roll dice, shuffle cards or pick a hero, and a simulation can repeat an experiment thousands of times in a second.
topics.teach: Explain why computer “random” numbers are really pseudo-random.
topics.talk: Ask {him} how a simulation could estimate the chance of rolling a double six.

topics.title: Bug hunting: harder debugging
topics.intro: Logic errors are the hardest bugs: the program runs, but the answer is wrong. Good debuggers compare what the program does with what it should do, then find the exact line where they part ways.
topics.teach: Explain what an off-by-one error is.
topics.talk: Show {him} a bug from your own work and ask how {she} would find it.

topics.title: Tracing algorithms step by step
topics.intro: Knowing the name of an algorithm is not enough: you need to be able to follow it step by step, like a computer would. Trace tables and careful notes make it reliable.
topics.teach: Explain the steps of a binary search for one number.
topics.talk: Ask {her} to sort a shuffled hand of cards using insertion sort and narrate it.

topics.title: Algorithm efficiency
topics.intro: Two algorithms can give the same answer but take wildly different times. Computer scientists count steps and describe how the work grows as the data grows, using Big-O notation: O(n), O(n²), O(log n).
topics.teach: Explain why an O(n²) algorithm gets slow on big lists.
topics.talk: Ask {him} how many handshakes there are if everyone in a class shakes hands once.

topics.title: Stacks, queues and arrays
topics.intro: A stack is last in, first out, like a pile of plates. A queue is first in, first out, like the line at a ticket office. These simple structures power undo buttons, printers and even how a program calls functions.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between a stack and a queue, with an example of each.
topics.talk: Ask {her} whether the “back” button in a web browser is a stack or a queue.

topics.title: Compression
topics.intro: Compression makes files smaller so they download faster and take less space. Lossless compression gives back exactly the original; lossy compression throws away detail people will not notice.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between lossy and lossless compression.
topics.talk: Compare the file size of a photo and a screenshot on your phone together.

topics.title: Encryption: Vigenère and public keys
topics.intro: The Caesar cipher has only 25 keys, so it is easy to crack. The Vigenère cipher uses a key word, so each letter is shifted by a different amount. Modern public-key encryption lets strangers send secrets without ever meeting to share a key.
topics.teach: Explain why the Vigenère cipher is harder to crack than the Caesar cipher.
topics.talk: Send each other a Vigenère message at dinner.

topics.title: How the internet works
topics.intro: When you visit a website, your device asks a DNS server for the site’s IP address, then sends a request in packets that hop between routers across the world. The answer comes back the same way, often in under a second.
topics.teach: Explain what happens, step by step, when you type a web address.
topics.talk: Ask {him} how a message gets from your house to a server in another country.

topics.title: The web: HTML and CSS
topics.intro: Every web page is made of HTML (the structure and content), CSS (the style) and often JavaScript (the behaviour). Reading markup is like reading the scaffolding behind the page.
topics.teach: Explain the jobs of HTML and CSS.
topics.talk: Open “view source” on a simple web page together and find the <h1>.

topics.title: Databases in depth
topics.intro: Databases answer questions about huge amounts of data in moments. SQL can count, total, sort and search, and a primary key makes sure every record can be found exactly.
topics.teach: Explain what COUNT(*) and ORDER BY do.
topics.talk: Ask {her} what tables a school database would need.

topics.title: Artificial intelligence and machine learning
topics.intro: Machine learning systems are not programmed with rules: they learn patterns from huge amounts of training data. That makes them powerful, and also means they can copy the mistakes and biases in the data.
topics.teach: Explain how bias can get into an AI system.
topics.talk: Ask {him} where {she} has met AI today, and whether it was always right.

topics.title: Inside the CPU
topics.intro: Inside the CPU, a clock ticks billions of times a second, registers hold the values being worked on, and fast cache memory keeps useful data close. More cores let a CPU work on several things at once.
topics.teach: Explain three things that affect how fast a CPU is.
topics.talk: Look up the clock speed and number of cores of a device at home.

topics.title: Operating systems and utilities
topics.intro: The operating system is the manager: it shares out memory and processor time, talks to devices through drivers, keeps files organised and keeps users apart. Utilities are small programs that look after the computer.
topics.teach: Explain three jobs an operating system does.
topics.talk: Ask {her} which operating systems are on the devices in your home.

topics.title: Law, ethics and the environment in depth
topics.intro: Technology changes lives, so laws and ethics matter: who may use your data, what counts as hacking, who owns a piece of music, and what happens to the millions of devices thrown away every year.
topics.teach: Explain one principle of the Data Protection Act.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what {she} would put in a law about AI.

topics.title: Recursion
topics.intro: A recursive function calls itself, each time on a smaller problem, until it reaches a base case it can answer directly. Like Russian dolls, or a hall of mirrors.
topics.teach: Explain why every recursive function needs a base case.
topics.talk: Ask {her} to explain recursion using a recursive explanation.

topics.title: Graphs and shortest paths
topics.intro: A graph is a set of places (nodes) joined by routes (edges), sometimes with distances. Breadth-first search finds the fewest steps through a labyrinth; Dijkstra’s algorithm finds the shortest weighted route, as a sat nav does.
topics.teach: Explain how breadth-first search finds the shortest route out of a maze.
topics.talk: Plan the quickest route between three places in town, as a graph.

topics.title: Logic circuits and Boolean expressions
topics.intro: Logic gates combine into circuits, and circuits can be written as Boolean expressions like (A AND B) OR C. A truth table proves exactly what a circuit does for every possible input.
topics.teach: Explain how to build a truth table for a three-input expression.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to design a circuit for a door alarm.

topics.title: Huffman coding
topics.intro: Huffman coding gives the most common characters the shortest codes, so text takes fewer bits. No code is the start of another, so a stream of bits can be read without gaps.
topics.teach: Explain why common letters get short Huffman codes.
topics.talk: Count the commonest letter in a page of a book together.

items.prompt: Evaluate this password policy for a school website: “Passwords must be 6 letters long. Users must change their password every week, and may write it on a sticky note.”
hints: Judge each part of the policy, not just one
Explain why length and variety matter (brute-force and guessing attacks)
Explain the human problem with weekly changes and sticky notes
Suggest a better policy
items.model: The policy is weak. Six letters is far too short: a computer can try every combination quickly in a brute-force attack, and letters only gives fewer possibilities than mixing letters, digits and symbols. Weekly changes sound secure but make people choose simple, predictable passwords, and allowing sticky notes means anyone walking past can read them. A better policy would require long passphrases (for example three random words and a number), no forced weekly changes, a lock-out after several wrong attempts, and two-factor authentication, while never writing the password down where others can see it.

items.prompt: Explain why binary search is so much faster than linear search for large lists, and give one situation where linear search is the better choice.

items.model: Linear search may have to check every item, so a list of a million names could take a million comparisons. Binary search checks the middle item and throws away half of the list each time, so a million items need only about 20 checks, and doubling the list adds just one more. However, binary search only works on a sorted list. If the list is unsorted and you only need to search it once, or it is very small, linear search is better, because sorting it first would take longer than simply checking each item.

items.prompt: Explain how public-key encryption solves the problem of sharing a secret key with someone you have never met.
hints: Explain the problem: with one shared key, the key itself has to be sent safely

items.model: With a symmetric cipher such as Vigenère, both people need the same key, but sending the key is risky: anyone who intercepts it can read every message. Public-key encryption uses a pair of keys. The public key can be shared with everyone and is used to encrypt, but only the matching private key, which never leaves its owner, can decrypt. It is like handing out open padlocks: anyone can lock a box, but only you can open it. When you buy something online, your browser uses the shop’s public key to agree a secret session key safely, so strangers can communicate securely.

items.model: First the browser asks a DNS server to translate www.example.org into the server’s IP address. It then sends an HTTP (or HTTPS, encrypted) request for the page. The request is split into packets, each labelled with the destination address, and routers pass them from network to network until they reach the server. The server sends the page back, also in packets, which may take different routes and are reassembled in order. Finally the browser reads the HTML, CSS and any JavaScript and draws the page on the screen.

items.model: A primary key is a field whose value is different for every record, so each vase can be identified exactly. items.prompt: Theo says: “A computer with twice as many cores will always run my game twice as fast.” Explain whether he is right.

items.model: Theo is not right. Each core can run instructions at the same time as the others, so more cores help when work can be split into independent parts. But many parts of a game depend on each other and must happen in order, and the game has to be written to use several cores at all, so the extra cores may sit idle.
